text: While meeting someone with a first name like 'Brooklyn' might pretty typical today, it would be unusual in Vietnam-era US. Referring to people by their last name (or rank - last name) is standard in the military for practical reasons. A soldier's last name was displayed on their uniform. In any random group of people, it's a lot more likely two people will have the same first name than the same last name. You don't want to be in the middle of a skirmish and yell out 'John, cover me' and have multiple people think you are talking to them. But they might also get a nickname. If you had one guy from Texas in your unit, it would be very normal to call him 'Tex'. Why? Texas has a more unique culture than most states in the US. It's one of only six (well 5 and a half) states in the US that was an independent nation. The prior independence other 5.5 states as nations is pretty obscure, but Texas tends to celebrate that independent history and it is well-known ("remember the Alamo".) […]

text: A lot of time units in our own world are based on cyclical events: A year is the time it takes the Earth to fully revolve around the Sun. Even in historic times when people did not understand that the Earth revolves around the Sun, they could still observe that the Sun would sometimes be higher and sometimes be lower above the horizon, or that the days would get longer and shorter, and you could use these cycles to define a year. A day is the time it takes the Earth to fully revolve around itself. Again, even without understanding that the Earth is a sphere (more specifically, an oblate spheroid) and that it rotates, there are still cyclical events happening that you can observe, most obviously, day and night. A month is (very roughly) the time it takes for the Moon to go from a New Moon to a Full Moon and back. All of these things also happen on other planets that rotate, revolve around the Sun, and have moons. […]

text: There's a legal disposition in French law called "convention d'occupation précaire"1 (roughly translated as "precarious/tenuous occupancy agreement"). It says that some people (landlords) may agree to let other people occupy their home for a short period of time under that "precarious occupancy agreement". This means that the 'tenants' (for lack of a better word, because legally, they're not!) will pay some bills for the time spent and take care of the house/apartment. They will not pay rent, making this an agreement and not a lease. Rights (and laws) differentiate between the two. Original: Pour qu’un engagement soit qualifié de convention précaire et non de bail, le propriétaire doit justifier d’une raison qui lui avait permis de concéder à titre précaire l’occupation du logement. text: Mr. Nev is an insurance agent, who will likely receive a commission for a successful policy sale and possibly a promotion. However, Mr. Nev is also suspicious of this policy: typically a life insurance policy is established with the policy holder's involvement, so it looks suspicious when the holder is not involved at all. Catherine, meanwhile, wants to stall for time because she also finds the policy irregular. In fact, once she realises that Mr. Nev is wary of the policy but hopes to proceed anyway, she ventures that Mr. Nev values the signing of the policy rather than her own wellbeing. Her use of the word "ambitious" here is hence a euphemism for his desire to benefit at any cost, including her own; his desire to benefit within the company, rather than to maintain for her wellbeing.
label: reasoned
author: Zoltar

text: Ansel Adams, the famous photographer, once said: "I would never apologize for photographing rocks. Rocks can be very beautiful. But, yes, people have asked why I don’t put people into my pictures of the natural scene. I respond, there are always two people in every picture: the photographer and the viewer." In this case, Robin Williams' character is in the photograph: he took it, and he is showing us, the viewer, how he sees that memory; later, his painting of the boat, according to Will Hunting, also shows us how Robin Williams sees the memory of his wife.
label: reasoned
notes: Reasoned. Adams's quote introduces an analogy about photography. It does not establish the interpretation of the character's memories.
